summary: 1. High-stayed videos (>50% stayed_pct) address immediate human experiences (eyes, onions) or famous pop-culture myths (T. rex), whereas low-stayed videos focus on complex astronomy or highway engineering. 2. Winning first sentences instantly make a provocative assertion directly addressing the viewer ('Your eyes are leaking right now') rather than building slow setup background ('Fossilized bones can last...'). 3. Top titles are short, question/curiosity-driven, and under 7 words ('Could A T. rex Outrun Your Car?'), while low-performing titles rely on abstract science phrasing. 4. Subverting expectations in the very first sentence ('Not even a jog', 'You are not sad') prevents early swiping far better than generic mystery hooks ('Most James Webb images hold secrets'). 5. Scriptwriters must cut all contextual preamble and state the shocking contradiction within the first 5 words.
winning_hooks: Direct viewer subversion: 'Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.'
Immediate myth-busting: 'The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.'
Bold short contradiction: 'You are not sad when you chop an onion.'
avoid: Slow background setups: 'Fossilized bones can last millions of years, but sometimes...'
Passive scenario building: 'Your car swerves off the highway right toward...'
Vague high-level claims: 'Most James Webb images hold secrets.'
next_experiment: Test Hook Type A (Direct bold contradiction: 'Your brain shuts off your vision 40 minutes a day') vs Hook Type B (Scenario setup: 'If you look in the mirror right now, something strange happens') using the exact same body video on body science topics.
